title: Scams, Deception & Social Engineering
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: A sign used to make a speaker appear legitimate or powerful.
glossary.example: A caller says they work in the bank's fraud department and quotes card details.
glossary.limit: A convincing detail does not prove that the caller is authorised.

glossary.definition: A demand to act quickly, often before there is time to check independently.
glossary.example: The caller says the account will be emptied in five minutes.
glossary.limit: Real problems can be urgent; independent verification is still important.

glossary.definition: Checking a claim through a channel chosen separately from the person making it.
glossary.example: Someone hangs up and calls the number printed on their bank card.
glossary.limit: Following a link supplied by the suspicious caller is not independent checking.

glossary.definition: Using human trust and decision-making patterns to obtain information or actions.
glossary.example: A fraudster uses fear of a lost bank balance to obtain a transfer.
glossary.limit: Susceptibility to a carefully timed message is not a measure of intelligence.

nodes.title: What authority cue means
nodes.body:
A sign used to make a speaker appear legitimate or powerful.

For example: A caller says they work in the bank's fraud department and quotes card details.

One important limit: A convincing detail does not prove that the caller is authorised.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Alina receives a call claiming to be from her bank's fraud department. Rob is with her.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.
nodes.scenario: Alina receives a call claiming to be from her bank's fraud department. Rob is with her.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They said someone is transferring money from my account right now.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did you call the bank, or did the call come to you?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They called me. They knew the last four digits of my card.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What are they asking you to do?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
checks.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Contact the institution using a verified channel you choose rather than contact details supplied by the caller. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Contact the institution using a verified channel you choose rather than contact details supplied by the caller.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Alina ends the call and uses the number printed on her card. The bank confirms there is no outgoing transfer and the 'safe account' instruction was fraudulent.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: Independent verification directly resolves the central claim and shows why the caller's instructions should not have been treated as authoritative.
nodes.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: The deadline that isn't yours
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of time pressure and cognitive overload.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre, suspicious messages and social engineering guidance.
nodes.scenario: Alex receives a delivery text saying a parcel will be returned unless a small fee is paid within fifteen minutes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: This text says my parcel is going back tonight.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Yes. It has a payment link and a countdown.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you checked the order outside the message?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not yet. I feel like waiting means I'll lose it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: The deadline may be making verification seem riskier than paying.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: The imposed deadline may be discouraging independent verification before a payment.
A courier may genuinely have a time-sensitive delivery problem.
Alex's earlier parcel problems may be driving the worry more than the countdown.
The caller may know accurate account details because those were obtained from a previous data leak.
options.feedback: Specific knowledge can increase apparent credibility without establishing legitimacy.

options.label: The caller’s demand for secrecy may be intended to prevent the independent verification that would expose the deception.
options.feedback: This is consistent with discouraging contact through trusted channels.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. The imposed deadline may be discouraging independent verification before a payment. A courier may genuinely have a time-sensitive delivery problem. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.

checks.prompt: You are Alex. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: Have you checked the order outside the message?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: Close the text and open the retailer or courier's own site or app to check the order.
options.reply: That check is stronger evidence than the threat in the text.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Pay the small fee first and dispute it later if the parcel does not arrive.
options.reply: The deadline may be making verification seem riskier than paying.
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: The caller may know accurate account details because those were obtained from a previous data leak.
options.feedback: Specific knowledge can increase apparent credibility without establishing legitimacy.

checks.explanation: The first response addresses what can change. Asking about motives may help eventually; it need not be resolved before the concrete issue can be addressed.
checks.counterexample: Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.

nodes.title: Find the evidence
nodes.prompt: Which two statements most directly support the working explanation?
nodes.explanation: The most informative lines reveal what the situation means to the speaker. They suggest that the imposed deadline may be discouraging independent verification before a payment. Other remarks establish circumstances, which can matter without revealing a psychological process.
nodes.counterexample: Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre, suspicious messages and social engineering guidance.

Social engineering can change the conditions under which someone decides. Time pressure makes caution seem expensive, while a small fee lowers the apparent cost of compliance. The safer test is to leave the supplied link and verify through a trusted, independently accessed channel.

Some real services do have deadlines. Urgency alone justifies verification; it does not prove fraud.

options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: Keep the caller talking until you feel completely certain they are lying.

options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Contact the institution using a verified channel you choose rather than contact details supplied by the caller.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

options.label: Examine whether a similar response occurs when the immediate practical stakes are different.
options.feedback: A pattern could test generalisation, although the settings may not be comparable.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
An urgent message supposedly from a university asks a student to enter a password through a link before a scholarship offer expires.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

options.label: End the unsolicited call and contact the bank through the number on your card or its trusted app.
options.feedback: This may be helpful at another stage. We still need a response that fits the practical aim and the current evidence.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Authority cues and urgency narrow the space for deliberation. A claimed emergency is used to make independent verification feel costly.

Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

glossary.definition: A sign used to make a speaker appear legitimate or powerful.
glossary.example: A caller says they work in the bank's fraud department and quotes card details.
glossary.limit: A convincing detail does not prove that the caller is authorised.

glossary.definition: A demand to act quickly, often before there is time to check independently.
glossary.example: The caller says the account will be emptied in five minutes.
glossary.limit: Real problems can be urgent; independent verification is still important.

glossary.definition: Checking a claim through a channel chosen separately from the person making it.
glossary.example: Someone hangs up and calls the number printed on their bank card.
glossary.limit: Following a link supplied by the suspicious caller is not independent checking.

glossary.definition: Using human trust and decision-making patterns to obtain information or actions.
glossary.example: A fraudster uses fear of a lost bank balance to obtain a transfer.
glossary.limit: Susceptibility to a carefully timed message is not a measure of intelligence.
